previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (what next) I'd rather use GDB for logging than for stepping. Stepping through Lean's startup would mean following about 900 initialization functions one call at a time, which is too slow to port from. What the port has to reproduce is what those calls leave behind: the parser tables, the token table, the attribute and extension registries. So I propose three steps. First, dump that state from real Lean right after initialization. Second, dump the same state from the port at the matching point. Third, list every difference between the two. That list becomes the fix curriculum, known in advance. GDB comes in when one difference needs locating. Shall I start step 1 with codex-5?

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: (where GDB fits) Lean's compiled functions are ordinary C symbols (`l_Lean_Parser_addBuiltinParser` and so on). That means we can set scripted breakpoints on the few registration functions and log each call's arguments in order, calling Lean's own `Name.toString` from GDB to print them. That gives the exact sequence in which Lean registers things. We'd use it when a dump difference depends on order, such as parser priority or which alias wins. The callgrind files already hold caller-to-callee edges, so some of those questions can be answered without GDB.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text:
(order of work)
1. codex-5 writes a Lean program that runs after initialization and writes canonical TSVs of each registry, with a self-check against facts we already know (the 73 aliases, `namedName` in its category). It's read-only and goes in `lean-wiring`.
2. A Kimi agent gets the port to write the same TSVs at the end of its startup.
3. A diff of the two becomes the fix list, one dispatch per group.
